title: Limits with Love
reflection: Which one or two rules in my home truly matter, and how could I explain each so that my child sees its purpose?

questions.q: According to Lesson 12, how does discipline differ from punishment?
o: Discipline is the stricter of the two, and punishment is the gentler of the two.
Discipline is for older children, and punishment is for the younger ones.
Punishment only restrains and denies; discipline teaches and trains the buddhi.
Discipline comes from the parent, and punishment comes from life itself.
questions.e: Discipline shares its root with “disciple”, one who learns. Punishment only restrains and denies; discipline teaches. It trains and strengthens the buddhi, the inner power to discern the true from the false, and the strength to govern oneself. Rules are the embankments of a child’s life: they give the river its course.
questions.c: Discipline teaches; rules are the banks that give the river its course

questions.q: A seventeen-year-old objects that a curfew is only there to make her hate her mother. Which response fits Lesson 12?
o: Say that the rule is final and needs no reasons, since reasons only invite a debate.
Give way this once, so that she does not feel that love has been withdrawn.
Say that she will understand when she has children of her own.
Explain patiently why the no serves her good in the long run, and that it is given in love.
questions.e: A parent strengthens a child’s will through a loving no, and by patiently explaining why that no serves the child’s good in the long run. Little by little the child learns to accept, then to cooperate, and at last to appreciate what the parents are training them for. The no is itself an act of love.
questions.c: A loving no, explained, is itself an act of love

questions.q: In the lesson’s picture, what does a child learn when a tired parent keeps giving way?
o: That the parent’s love for him is greater than the parent’s wish for rules.
That limits bend if one only waits, so the embankment becomes a sandbank.
That the parent trusts him to look after himself, and he rises to meet it.
That the rules of the home are for the family to keep, and not for him.
questions.e: When order slides into heavy inertia, tiredness or the wish to avoid one more struggle makes the parent give way, and the rule announced on Monday is forgotten by Wednesday. The child learns that limits bend if one only waits, and the embankment becomes a sandbank that the water simply washes away. None of this is cause for shame.
questions.c: A home that slips into tamas lets the loving duty go undone

questions.q: A father raised his voice while holding a limit, and the child is upset. Which repair fits Lesson 12?
o: Drop the rule, since it was held in anger and cannot be fair.
Say sorry for the rule as well as for the shouting, so that the bond is fully restored.
Say nothing of it, since the child will see that the limit still stands.
Say, “I raised my voice, and that was not right. The rule still stands.”
questions.e: When the calm has been lost, it can be repaired simply: “I raised my voice, and that was not right. The rule still stands.” Both the bond and the limit are restored. Warmth and firmness are not opposites: the warmth is for the child, the firmness is about the boundary, and the child is never rejected; only the action is declined.
questions.c: Repair the calm and keep the limit

questions.q: “Warmth and firmness are opposites, so a parent has to choose which one a child needs most.”
questions.e: Warmth and firmness are not opposites. A river’s embankments are firm, and it is their very firmness that lets the water travel far and flow freely. A parent can be wholly loving toward the child and wholly steady about the limit, because the no is itself an act of love.

questions.q: A father either shouts or gives in, and his seven-year-old says, “He always gets his way.” Which approach fits Lesson 12?
o: Add more rules, so that each one is less likely to be crossed.
Raise his voice at the first sign of a challenge, so that the limit is clear.
Offer a small reward each time a rule is kept, so that it is kept more gladly.
Hold only a few rules that matter, and say each one once, calmly, and keep it.
questions.e: Return to the few rules that truly matter: those that guard safety, health, respect for others and the child’s growth. Say each one once, calmly and clearly, and keep it. The more rules are added, the less each one means; the calmest teacher is the one whose limits are said once and kept.
questions.c: A few clear rules, said once and kept

questions.q: A seventeen-year-old stays out past the agreed time, and her mother feels frightened and angry. Which response fits Lesson 12?
o: Ground her at once for a month, so the lesson is not forgotten for a long time.
Treat it as defiance, and tighten every rule until she keeps all of them.
Let her own storm pass first, then talk it through when both are calm, and agree on next time.
Let it pass without a word, since it happened only once and nothing came of it.
questions.e: A crossed limit is feedback: often the strength to keep it has not yet grown. Better first to regain one’s own self-control and let the storm pass. Then, when both hearts are quiet, talk it through and agree how to meet it better next time, and start with: “Tell me what happened. If it’s the truth, you’re forgiven, and we’ll learn from it.”
questions.c: A crossed limit is feedback; honesty is met with forgiveness

questions.q: “A smack, or harsh punishment, teaches a child where the limit lies faster than words do.”
questions.e: Harsh punishment, humiliation and a smack so often fail to teach; they leave scars of hurt and of fear, and a child who fears the consequence may learn to hide the truth. What has passed can still be spoken of and repaired. If a home ever feels unsafe, please reach out to a doctor or a local helpline.

questions.q: According to Lesson 12, what does it mean when a young person keeps a discipline only while someone is watching?
o: The parent’s rules were too weak, and should have been made stricter.
The young person has chosen to turn against the family’s values for good.
The discipline was not really worth keeping, and so fell away of itself.
Self-control has not yet grown strong enough; it is not a judgment on anyone.
questions.e: Practised day after day, each limit leaves its impression in the child’s mind, until it is no longer outside at all. When a young person keeps a discipline only while watched, the saṁskāras of self-control had not yet grown strong enough. It is a measure of strength still to be gathered, not a judgement on anyone.
questions.c: Over the years the banks become a channel within

questions.q: A parent of a fifteen-year-old wants the family’s rules to become the young person’s own. Which approach fits Lesson 12?
o: Write the rules down clearly, so that there can be no dispute about what they are.
Add a new rule each time she shows that she cannot keep an earlier one.
Wait until she is a good deal older before giving any reasons for them.
Draw her into making the rules, let her propose some, and trust her with more.
questions.e: As children grow, parents can empower them by drawing them into the decisions about what is good for them: inviting them to help make the rules, letting them carry real responsibility, and entrusting them, step by step, with more. Each step of trust says, “We believe you can.”
questions.c: Draw children into making the rules
